questions.p:
Jacob, 12, has 3 weeks of a swelling belly, abdominal pain and vomiting. His family thought it was appendicitis because the pain began in the right lower abdomen. He had mononucleosis a year ago. His uncle had follicular lymphoma. He has lost 3 kg.

He has had no fevers or night sweats. He is passing less urine than usual. He takes no medications.

Review of systems: no diarrhea, blood in stool, cough or bone pain. He is in grade 7 and plays hockey. He was born at term and has had no prior illnesses apart from mono.

Vitals: HR 112, BP 112/70, T 37.2°C.
Exam: Distended abdomen with a large, firm right lower quadrant mass. No peripheral nodes.

CT: large mass in the right lower abdomen.

Hb 118 g/L (ref 115-155)
WBC 9.6 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 340 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
LDH very high
Uric acid high
Biopsy: sheets of medium-sized B cells with scattered macrophages giving a starry-sky pattern, and very high mitotic activity.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: A. A child with a fast-growing abdominal mass, a very high LDH and a starry-sky pattern has Burkitt lymphoma, from t(8;14) with c-Myc activation.
B: DLBCL shows sheets of large cells without a starry-sky pattern.
C: ALL presents with blasts in the blood and marrow failure.
D: Anaplastic large cell lymphoma has t(2;5) with ALK1.
E: Follicular lymphoma is indolent and seen in older adults.
Red herring: The right lower quadrant pain tempts appendicitis, and his uncle's follicular lymphoma tempts the same diagnosis. A starry-sky pattern with very high mitotic activity in a child means Burkitt lymphoma.
Takeaway: Watch for tumour lysis syndrome when treatment starts.

questions.p:
Four children are referred to a pediatric lymph node clinic. Their parents are worried because each child's node is large or long-lasting. The 7-year-old has the largest node, at 2.5 cm.

Which child most needs further workup for possible malignancy?
o: A 4-year-old with small neck nodes and an ear infection
A newborn with a 1.5 cm non-tender neck node
A 5-year-old with tender neck nodes and a sore throat
A 7-year-old whose 2.5 cm node shrank on antibiotics
questions.e:
Correct: B. Non-tender nodes over 1 cm with onset in the neonatal period are a listed concerning feature.
A: Small nodes with an ear infection fit a reactive cause.
C: Tender nodes with throat symptoms suggest an infection, and ENT symptoms are reassuring.
D: Nodes of 2 cm or more are concerning when they grow or fail to resolve after 2 weeks of antibiotics. This one shrank.
Red herring: The 7-year-old has the biggest node, but it shrank on antibiotics, which points to infection. A non-tender node over 1 cm in a newborn is a listed concerning feature.
Takeaway: In children, benign causes are more likely the younger the child, except in the neonatal period.

questions.p:
Walter, 66, has a 2 cm neck node. The ENT surgeon is busy, so a radiologist does a fine needle aspirate in clinic. It is quick and cheap, and it shows many small lymphocytes. The hematologist is not satisfied with the result.

Which limitation of FNA matters most here?
o: It must be done by a surgeon in an operating room
It is the most expensive of the three sampling methods
It loses the architecture, so lymphoma cannot be sub-classified
It carries the highest infection risk of all the sampling options available
questions.e:
Correct: C. FNA gives no nodal architecture, so it cannot sub-classify lymphoma. It also cannot separate benign from malignant low grade LPD.
A: FNA needs no surgeon and no OR.
B: FNA is the least expensive option.
D: FNA has a lower risk of infection and complications.
Red herring: Speed and cost sound like the issue, but FNA is fast and cheap. The problem is that it loses node architecture, so lymphoma cannot be sub-classified.
Takeaway: FNA is easy and cheap but cannot show architecture.

questions.p:
Raymond, 38, noticed a painless lump in his right neck 6 months ago that has grown slowly. He had a dental abscess on the right side 2 months ago. He has itchy skin after hot showers. His brother had nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma.

He has had no fevers, night sweats or weight loss. He runs marathons.

Review of systems: no cough, chest pain, abdominal pain or bone pain. He takes no medications. He works as a high school teacher and does not smoke.

Vitals: HR 58, BP 120/76.
Exam: Two firm, non-tender nodes in the right neck. No other nodes. No spleen.

CT: only two enlarged nodes in the right neck.

Hb 148 g/L (ref 135-170)
WBC 7.2 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 260 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
LDH normal
Node biopsy: nodular architecture with large cells that have a popcorn appearance, arising from germinal centre B cells.
Stains: CD20 and CD45 positive, CD15 and CD30 negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: D. Popcorn cells that are CD20 and CD45 positive and CD15 and CD30 negative, in a nodular pattern, with early-stage disease and no B symptoms, fit NLPHL, 5% of HL.
A: Nodular sclerosis shows lacunar cells that are CD15 and CD30 positive and CD20 negative.
B: SLL is a disease of older adults with smudge cells and blood involvement.
C: Follicular lymphoma has a follicular pattern without popcorn cells.
E: DLBCL is a rapidly enlarging mass with loss of node structure.
Red herring: His brother's nodular sclerosis HL tempts the same type, but nodular sclerosis is CD15 and CD30 positive. The dental abscess tempts reactive nodes. Popcorn cells that are CD20 positive and CD15 and CD30 negative mean NLPHL.
Takeaway: NLPHL: mostly early stage, indolent, with an excellent prognosis.

questions.p:
Ingrid, 60, has a lymphoma that the pathology report calls aggressive. Imaging shows involved nodes in her neck and groin, on both sides of the diaphragm. Her marrow is clear. Her husband asks whether "aggressive" means it has spread everywhere.

Which interpretation is correct?
o: Aggressive describes the stage. Both sides of the diaphragm describes its grade
Aggressive describes clinical behaviour. Both sides of the diaphragm is stage II
Aggressive means stage IV. Both sides of the diaphragm confirms bone marrow disease
Aggressive describes clinical behaviour. Both sides of the diaphragm is stage III
questions.e:
Correct: D. Indolent, aggressive and very aggressive describe clinical behaviour. Ann Arbor staging describes spread, and nodes on both sides of the diaphragm is stage III.
A: This swaps behaviour and stage.
B: Stage II stays on one side of the diaphragm.
C: Stage IV means diffuse extralymphatic involvement, and behaviour is not a stage.
Red herring: Her husband links "aggressive" with spread, which tempts you to merge grade and stage. Aggressive describes behaviour. Nodes on both sides of the diaphragm is stage III.
Takeaway: Behaviour describes the tumour. Stage describes where it is.

questions.p:
Two patients have DLBCL. Gene expression profiling shows Patient 1 has the germinal centre B-cell type and Patient 2 has the activated B-cell type. Both are 60 and have the same stage. A third patient, with follicular lymphoma, asks how her risk is scored.

Which statement about prognosis in non-Hodgkin lymphoma is correct?
o: DLBCL of germinal centre type does better than activated B-cell type
Follicular lymphoma is risk scored with the standard IPI and nothing else
CLL caught early has a median survival of only 1 to 2 years
DLBCL is indolent and is usually incurable with treatment
questions.e:
Correct: A. DLBCL has a better prognosis if it is of germinal centre B-cell type rather than activated B-cell type.
B: Follicular lymphoma uses the FLIPI.
C: Median survival in CLL is 10 to 15 years if caught early.
D: DLBCL is aggressive but responds well to treatment.
Red herring: The follicular lymphoma patient tempts you toward the standard IPI, but follicular lymphoma has its own index. DLBCL of germinal centre type does better than activated B-cell type.
Takeaway: IPI for DLBCL, FLIPI for follicular.

questions.p:
Harold, 68, had a serum protein electrophoresis during a workup for mild fatigue, which showed an M protein. He sleeps poorly because of his new grandchild. He had a kidney stone 5 years ago. He has mild back stiffness in the mornings that eases with walking. His brother has myeloma.

He has had no bone pain, infections or weight loss. He takes no medications.

Review of systems: no cough, chest pain, numbness or tingling, and no blood in his urine. He is a retired teacher who walks daily. He does not smoke and drinks a glass of wine with dinner.

Vitals: HR 70, BP 128/78.
Exam: Normal.

Hb 138 g/L (ref 135-170)
WBC 6.4 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 230 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Calcium 2.36 mmol/L
Creatinine 82 µmol/L
Marrow plasma cells 14%, monoclonal
Skeletal survey: no lytic lesions.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. Monoclonal plasma cells of 10% or more in the marrow with no CRAB organ damage and no symptoms is smoldering myeloma.
A: A plasmacytoma is a single tumour.
B: POEMS brings neuropathy, organomegaly, endocrine and skin changes.
C: Multiple myeloma needs organ damage.
D: MGUS has fewer than 10% plasma cells.
Red herring: His brother's myeloma, the old kidney stone and back stiffness tempt multiple myeloma. He has no CRAB features: calcium, creatinine and Hb are normal and there are no lytic lesions. Plasma cells of 10% or more without organ damage is smoldering myeloma.
Takeaway: Smoldering myeloma: close follow-up every 3 to 6 months.

questions.p:
Grace, 66, has multiple myeloma. Her friend with follicular lymphoma was treated with rituximab and did well, and Grace asks why she is getting daratumumab instead.

Why is daratumumab, and not rituximab, used as an antibody therapy in multiple myeloma?
o: Rituximab targets CD38, which plasma cells do not carry
Plasma cells lack CD20, and daratumumab targets CD38
Plasma cells lack CD38, so only a CD20 antibody works
Daratumumab targets the CD20 that plasma cells carry
questions.e:
Correct: B. Plasma cells do not express CD20, the target of rituximab. Daratumumab targets CD38 and is listed for myeloma.
A: Rituximab targets CD20.
C: Plasma cells do not express CD20, so a CD20 antibody would miss them.
D: Daratumumab targets CD38, and plasma cells do not carry CD20.
Red herring: Her friend's success with rituximab tempts you to think it would work. Plasma cells lack CD20. Daratumumab targets CD38.
Takeaway: Rituximab is for B-cell lymphomas. Daratumumab is for myeloma.

questions.p:
Arthur, 63, has had painless lumps in his neck, armpits and groin for over a year. They come and go in size. He had a cold last month, and his nodes seemed bigger during it. He was treated for latent TB 20 years ago. His granddaughter has a cat that scratches him.

He feels well, with no fevers or weight loss. He walks daily.

Review of systems: no cough, abdominal pain, itching or bleeding. He worked as a farmer for 30 years. He does not smoke. His wife is well.

Vitals: HR 74, BP 130/80.
Exam: Rubbery nodes in the neck, armpits and groin. Palpable spleen tip.

Hb 124 g/L (ref 135-170)
WBC 4.6 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 142 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
LDH normal
Node biopsy: a follicular pattern of small B cells.
Cytogenetics: t(14;18).

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. Widespread painless nodes in an older adult with an indolent course, a follicular pattern and t(14;18) with Bcl-2 activation fit follicular lymphoma, the second most common NHL.
A: Burkitt has t(8;14) and a starry-sky pattern.
B: DLBCL grows fast, with large cells and loss of node structure.
C: Mantle cell lymphoma has t(11;14) with cyclin D1.
D: NLPHL shows popcorn cells, not t(14;18).
Red herring: The cold, the cat and the old TB all offer benign causes of nodes. Waxing and waning widespread nodes with a follicular pattern and t(14;18) mean follicular lymphoma.
Takeaway: Follicular lymphoma: watch and wait until symptoms develop.

questions.p:
A family doctor sees four adults with lymphadenopathy in one week: one with a long fever and night sweats, one with a sore throat and a tender neck node, one with a node above the clavicle, and one who lost 12% of her weight.

Which findings in an adult with lymphadenopathy raise concern for malignancy?
i) Fever for more than 1 week with night sweats
ii) A tender 1 cm neck node with a sore throat
iii) A supraclavicular node
iv) Weight loss of more than 10% of body weight
questions.e:
Correct: C. Fever over 1 week, night sweats, weight loss over 10% and supraclavicular nodes are listed features concerning for malignancy.
A: A tender small node with throat symptoms is not a red flag. Absence of ENT symptoms is the concerning feature.
B: This leaves out the supraclavicular node, a listed red flag.
D: Statement ii) is not a concerning feature.
Red herring: Any node in an adult can feel worrying, but a tender node with a sore throat is the classic reactive pattern.
Takeaway: Red flags: B symptoms, supraclavicular, generalized, fixed or matted, abnormal CXR or CBC.

questions.p:
Jacob, 12, has a fast-growing abdominal mass with a very high LDH. Biopsy shows a starry-sky pattern. His uncle had follicular lymphoma, and the family asks if Jacob has "the same gene change".

Which genetic change is most likely?
questions.e:
Correct: A. A starry-sky pattern is the mark of Burkitt lymphoma, which carries t(8;14) and c-Myc activation.
B: t(11;14) with cyclin D1 is mantle cell lymphoma.
C: t(14;18) with Bcl-2 is follicular lymphoma.
D: t(2;5) with ALK1 is anaplastic large cell lymphoma.
Red herring: The uncle's follicular lymphoma tempts t(14;18). A starry-sky pattern means Burkitt lymphoma, with t(8;14) and c-Myc activation.
Takeaway: Starry sky means Burkitt means t(8;14).

questions.p:
Ruth, 72, has an M protein found on routine bloodwork done for her osteoporosis clinic. She has had a wrist fracture after a fall on ice. She has mild anemia from heavy NSAID use for arthritis, and her ferritin is low. She feels well otherwise.

She has had no bone pain, infections or weight loss.

Review of systems: no numbness, tingling, cough or blood in her urine. She takes alendronate, naproxen and a calcium supplement. She lives alone and still volunteers at her church.

Vitals: HR 76, BP 134/80.
Exam: Normal.

Hb 128 g/L (ref 115-160)
WBC 5.9 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 250 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Calcium 2.31 mmol/L
Creatinine 74 µmol/L
Marrow plasma cells 6%
Skeletal survey: no lytic lesions.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: B. An asymptomatic M protein with fewer than 10% marrow plasma cells and no organ damage is MGUS, with a 0.5 to 2% yearly risk of myeloma.
A: Myeloma needs organ damage.
C: Plasma cell leukemia needs plasma cells in the blood.
D: Smoldering myeloma needs 10% or more plasma cells.
E: AL amyloidosis brings organ damage from deposits.
Red herring: The wrist fracture tempts a myeloma bone lesion, but it followed a fall on ice and the skeletal survey is clear. Fewer than 10% plasma cells with no organ damage is MGUS.
Takeaway: MGUS: monitor 1 to 2 times a year.

questions.p:
Kerry, 30, will have radiation for early-stage Hodgkin lymphoma. Her nurse answers questions in a handout. One statement has crept in by mistake.

Which statement about radiation therapy for lymphoma is FALSE?
o: It carries a slight risk of a second cancer years later
It only treats tumour cells inside the radiation field
External beam treatment itself is painless
It damages only cancer cells and spares normal cells
questions.e:
Correct: D. Radiation damages the DNA of both normal and cancer cells. So the claim that it spares normal cells is false.
A: True. There is a slight risk of secondary cancer many years later.
B: True. Radiation only works on tumour cells in the field.
C: True. External beam radiation is painless.
Red herring: "Painless" and "slight second cancer risk" sound like the risky claims, but both are true. Radiation damages DNA in normal and cancer cells alike.
Takeaway: Every tissue has a dose limit. Spinal cord, bowel, kidney and lungs often limit treatment.

questions.p:
A pediatric resident sees many children with neck nodes. Her attending asks her to state one rule about lymphadenopathy in children before she orders more tests.

Which statement about lymphadenopathy in children is correct?
o: Lymphoid tissue mass peaks in early childhood
Palpable nodes are rare between ages 4 and 8
Benign causes are more likely the younger the child
Having ear, nose and throat symptoms makes malignancy more likely
questions.e:
Correct: C. Lymphadenopathy is common in children, and benign causes are more likely at a younger age.
A: Lymphoid tissue mass peaks in adolescence.
B: Lymphadenopathy is found in about 90% of children aged 4 to 8.
D: The absence of ENT symptoms is the concerning feature.
Red herring: ENT symptoms make a node feel more serious, but they point to infection. Benign causes are more likely the younger the child.
Takeaway: Peak lymphoid mass is in adolescence. Nodes are very common in young children.

questions.p:
Ruth, 72, has MGUS with fewer than 10% marrow plasma cells and no organ damage. Her daughter read that MGUS "turns into cancer" and wants her treated now. Ruth's friend had smoldering myeloma and was seen every few months.

Which follow-up plan and risk of progression to myeloma match the notes?
o: Monitor 1-2 times a year. Risk of myeloma is 0.5-2%
Start therapy now. Risk of myeloma is 0.5-2%
Give high dose chemotherapy as an emergency
Follow up every 3-6 months. Risk of myeloma is 5-25%
questions.e:
Correct: A. MGUS is monitored once or twice a year and carries a 0.5 to 2% risk of myeloma.
B: MGUS is asymptomatic and is monitored, not treated.
C: High dose combination chemotherapy is for plasma cell leukemia.
D: Follow-up every 3 to 6 months with a 5 to 25% risk is smoldering myeloma.
Red herring: Her friend's every-few-months follow-up and 5 to 25% risk belong to smoldering myeloma. MGUS is monitored once or twice a year, with a 0.5 to 2% risk.
Takeaway: MGUS is watched. Smoldering is watched more closely. Myeloma is treated.

questions.p:
A student writes four statements comparing Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma on a flashcard. She mixes up which lymphoma skips node groups.

Which statement comparing Hodgkin with non-Hodgkin lymphoma is FALSE?
o: All Hodgkin lymphoma is treated with the aim of cure
Hodgkin lymphoma often spreads in a non-contiguous pattern
Hodgkin lymphoma shows RS cells in an inflammatory background
Hodgkin lymphoma is usually nodal, and extranodal disease is rare
questions.e:
Correct: B. Hodgkin lymphoma spreads contiguously, from neck to supraclavicular, thorax and abdomen. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma can spread non-contiguously. So this statement is false.
A: True. All HL patients must be treated with the aim to cure.
C: True. RS cells in an inflammatory background are the HL hallmark.
D: True. HL is nodal, and extranodal disease is rare.
Red herring: "Non-contiguous" sounds like an aggressive feature that fits Hodgkin. Hodgkin spreads contiguously. Non-Hodgkin can skip.
Takeaway: HL: contiguous, nodal, RS cells, curable. NHL: varied spread, monoclonal.

questions.p:
Marcus, 52, has a 3 cm neck node and suspected lymphoma. He is a busy executive and asks for the quickest, least invasive test. The hematologist recommends a surgeon remove the whole node.

Which feature of an excisional biopsy makes it the most informative option?
o: It needs no surgeon and costs the least of the three options
It is the least invasive option and gives the fastest results
It shows the nodal architecture and gives no false negatives
It suits severely sick patients who cannot go to the OR
questions.e:
Correct: C. Excisional biopsy is always representative, has no false negatives and shows the architecture. It also gives enough tissue for every study.
A: No surgeon and lowest cost describe FNA.
B: Least invasive and fastest describe FNA.
D: Excisional biopsy cannot be done on severely sick compromised patients.
Red herring: His wish for the quickest test tempts FNA or core biopsy. Excisional biopsy is more invasive but shows architecture and has no false negatives.
Takeaway: Excisional biopsy is the most complete sample but needs a surgeon.

questions.p:
Two patients have lymphoma.

Patient A, a 22-year-old man, has nodes that spread in order from his neck to his mediastinum. He has itchy skin.

Patient B, a 70-year-old woman, has a lymphoma in her stomach and scattered nodes that skip node groups. She had H. pylori years ago.

Which type of lymphoma best fits each patient, in order?
questions.e:
Correct: D. Hodgkin lymphoma affects younger patients, mostly males, and spreads contiguously through nodes. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma affects older patients and can be extranodal and non-contiguous.
A: Patient A is young with contiguous nodal spread, which fits HL.
B: This reverses the age and spread patterns.
C: Patient B has extranodal disease in an older adult, which fits NHL.
Red herring: Itch and H. pylori are real associations but are not needed. Young, male and contiguous spread fits Hodgkin. Older, extranodal and non-contiguous fits non-Hodgkin.
Takeaway: Young, nodal and contiguous points to HL. Older and extranodal points to NHL.

questions.p:
Mia, 26, finished neck and mediastinal radiation for Hodgkin lymphoma. Over the next years, her doctor watches for effects. At 3 months she had tingling on neck flexion. At 2 years her TSH rose.

Which of these effects of radiation is classed as a late effect rather than a subacute one?
questions.e:
Correct: B. Hypothyroidism is listed as a late effect, and thyroid replacement is recommended.
A: L'Hermitte's sign is a subacute effect from transient demyelination.
C: Myelosuppression is subacute, after high volume pelvic marrow radiation.
D: Radiation pneumonitis is subacute, within 6 to 12 weeks.
Red herring: L'Hermitte's sign and pneumonitis both appear after radiation, which makes them tempting. They are subacute. Hypothyroidism is a late effect.
Takeaway: Late effects: hypothyroidism, zoster, infertility, secondary cancers.

questions.p:
Hana, 45, has enlarged nodes in her neck and in her right axilla. She had a viral illness 3 weeks ago, and the neck nodes are mildly tender. Her doctor calls the nodes "probably reactive".

How is her lymphadenopathy best classified?
questions.e:
Correct: C. Two separate anatomic areas are involved. More than one area is generalized, which raises concern for malignancy or another systemic condition.
A: Isolated means a single node.
B: Localized means one anatomic area.
D: Reactive is a cause, not a description of extent.
Red herring: The viral illness tempts "reactive", but that describes a cause, not the distribution. Two separate areas is generalized.
Takeaway: Isolated is one node, localized is one area, generalized is more than one area.

questions.p:
Chloe, 23, has 2 months of a dry cough, itchy skin and night sweats. She noticed a painless lump above her left collarbone. Her doctor first thought it was asthma and gave her an inhaler, which did not help. Her sister has myasthenia gravis. She had mono at 16.

She has lost 2 kg. She is a graduate student and does not smoke.

Review of systems: no chest pain, abdominal pain or bone pain. Her itch is worse at night and not linked to showers. She takes no medications apart from the inhaler.

Vitals: HR 96, BP 112/70, T 37.6°C.
Exam: Firm, painless left supraclavicular node. No wheeze. No spleen.

Chest X-ray: large anterior mediastinal mass.

Hb 122 g/L (ref 115-160)
WBC 10.8 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Eosinophils mildly high
Platelets 410 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
LDH normal
Node biopsy: Reed-Sternberg cells and lacunar cells in a nodular pattern with collagen bands, in a background of eosinophils, lymphocytes and plasma cells.
Stains: CD15 and CD30 positive, CD20 and CD45 negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. A young adult with a mediastinal mass, RS and lacunar cells, collagen bands, and a CD15 and CD30 positive, CD20 negative stain has nodular sclerosis HL, 70% of all HL.
A: Thymoma is a tumour of adults over 40 and is resected without a biopsy.
B: Lymphoblastic lymphoma comes on over days and shows immature blasts.
C: NLPHL shows popcorn cells that are CD20 positive and CD15 and CD30 negative, and rarely a mediastinal mass.
D: DLBCL has no Reed-Sternberg cells or inflammatory background.
Red herring: Her sister's myasthenia tempts thymoma, which is linked to myasthenia in the patient, not a relative. The past mono tempts EBV. Lacunar cells with collagen bands and CD15 and CD30 positivity mean nodular sclerosis HL.
Takeaway: Nodular sclerosis: mostly stage I to II, with a very good to excellent prognosis.

questions.p:
Imaging in a 50-year-old with back pain shows a mass in the posterior mediastinum beside the spine. He also has a history of a benign cyst near his heart found years ago, and he had myasthenia gravis in his 30s that resolved.

Which category of lesion is most likely?
questions.e:
Correct: D. The posterior paravertebral compartment holds the sympathetic trunk and nerves. Its differential is neurogenic tumours, meningoceles and spine lesions.
A: Bronchogenic cysts are middle compartment lesions.
B: Thymoma is an anterior compartment lesion.
C: Teratoma is an anterior compartment lesion.
Red herring: The old pericardial cyst and myasthenia tempt middle and anterior compartment lesions. The posterior paravertebral compartment holds nerves, so neurogenic tumours lead its differential.
Takeaway: Anterior 5Ts, middle nodes and cysts, posterior nerves.

questions.p:
Viktor, 66, has 4 months of swelling in his legs and shortness of breath on exertion. His tongue has grown larger, and his voice is hoarse. He has heavy protein in his urine. He had a heart attack 10 years ago. He takes amlodipine, which his doctor blames for the ankle swelling.

He has no bone pain. He does not smoke.

Review of systems: no fevers, night sweats or bone pain. He has noticed easy bruising around his eyes after coughing. He takes amlodipine and atorvastatin.

Vitals: HR 96, BP 104/66.
Exam: Enlarged tongue. Raised JVP. Pitting leg edema.
Echo: thick heart walls.

Hb 132 g/L (ref 135-170)
Platelets 240 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Calcium normal
Creatinine mildly high
Serum free light chains: monoclonal light chain excess
Fat pad biopsy: deposits of insoluble protein.
Skeletal survey: no lytic lesions.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. An abnormal light chain that becomes insoluble and deposits in the heart and kidneys, proven on biopsy, fits AL amyloidosis.
A: POEMS brings neuropathy, organomegaly, endocrine and skin changes.
B: Myeloma needs the CRAB pattern, and he has no lytic lesions, anemia or hypercalcemia.
C: MGUS has no organ damage.
D: Plasma cell leukemia needs plasma cells in the blood.
Red herring: Amlodipine and his old heart attack offer innocent explanations for swelling and heart failure. A large tongue, thick heart walls, proteinuria and insoluble protein deposits mean AL amyloidosis.
Takeaway: AL amyloidosis may be idiopathic, primary, or secondary to myeloma.

questions.p:
Jade, 22, has a tender lump in her right armpit for 10 days. Three weeks ago her new kitten scratched her right forearm, and a small bump formed at the scratch. Her mother had breast cancer at 45. Jade had a sore throat last month. She started a new antiepileptic drug 6 weeks ago.

She has a low-grade fever and no night sweats or weight loss.

Review of systems: no cough, rash, breast lumps or joint pain. She works at a vet clinic. She does not smoke and drinks socially.

Vitals: HR 88, T 37.8°C.
Exam: One tender, mobile 2.5 cm right axillary node. Healing papule on the right forearm. No other nodes or spleen. Normal breast exam.

Hb 134 g/L (ref 115-160)
WBC 9.8 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Lymphocytes normal
Platelets 270 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
LDH normal
Film: normal.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. A single tender, mobile axillary node draining a recent kitten scratch, with a normal CBC and film, fits cat-scratch disease, a listed cause of axillary nodes.
A: She takes no new drugs.
B: Hodgkin lymphoma gives painless nodes that spread in order.
C: Breast cancer nodes are usually fixed and painless, and she has a clear infectious source.
D: Mono causes sore throat, neck nodes and atypical lymphocytes.
Red herring: Her mother's breast cancer, the new antiepileptic and the sore throat all point elsewhere. A single tender node draining a recent kitten scratch with a papule fits cat-scratch disease.
Takeaway: Look at the area the node drains.

questions.p:
Sandra, 58, has a neck mass, and the radiologist plans an ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy rather than surgery. Sandra asks how reliable it will be.

Which statement about core needle biopsy of a lymph node is correct?
o: Results are best with 16-18 gauge needles plus flow cytometry
It is always representative and has no false negative results
It always yields enough tissue for cytogenetics and molecular work
It is usually performed by a surgeon in the operating room
questions.e:
Correct: A. Core biopsy works best with 16 to 18 gauge needles and a flow cytometry study.
B: Always representative with no false negatives describes excisional biopsy.
C: A limited core sample may be insufficient for cytogenetics and molecular studies.
D: Core biopsy is mostly performed by radiologists.
Red herring: "Always representative, no false negatives" sounds reassuring, but that describes excisional biopsy. Core biopsy works best with 16 to 18 gauge needles plus flow cytometry.
Takeaway: Core biopsy is the middle option between FNA and excision.

questions.p:
Walter, 69, has myeloma with back pain, two pneumonias this year, a high calcium and fatigue. A resident explains each symptom to his family.

Which explanations of myeloma symptoms match the notes?
i) Bone pain from an imbalance between osteoclasts and osteoblasts
ii) Infections from neutropenia and a weakened immune system
iii) Hypercalcemia from calcium released by damaged bones
iv) Fatigue caused only by high calcium
questions.e:
Correct: B. Bone pain, infections and hypercalcemia are explained as listed in the notes.
A: This leaves out infections, which come from neutropenia and weak immunity.
C: Fatigue has several causes, so iv) is wrong.
D: Statement iv) is wrong. Fatigue comes from anemia, psychological factors, drugs and infections.
Red herring: High calcium does cause fatigue, which makes iv) tempting. The word "only" makes it wrong.
Takeaway: CRAB features each have a mechanism you should be able to explain.

questions.p:
Gordon, 59, has 6 months of numbness and weakness in both feet, low libido and darkening of his skin. He has type 2 diabetes, which his family doctor blamed for the numbness. He drinks 4 beers a day. He has a tan from a recent holiday.

He has no bone pain or infections. He takes metformin.

Review of systems: no cough, chest pain or bleeding. He has noticed his breasts have grown slightly. He works as a mechanic.

Vitals: HR 80, BP 132/80.
Exam: Reduced sensation in a stocking pattern. Enlarged liver and spleen. Skin thickening and darkening.

Hb 142 g/L (ref 135-170)
Platelets 420 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Testosterone low
Serum M protein present
Calcium normal
Creatinine normal

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. Polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, an M protein and skin changes spell POEMS syndrome.
A: Smoldering myeloma has no organ involvement.
B: AL amyloidosis deposits in organs such as the heart and kidneys, without this endocrine and skin pattern.
C: Myeloma needs CRAB organ damage, and his calcium, creatinine and Hb are normal.
D: MGUS has no organ involvement.
Red herring: Diabetes explains neuropathy, alcohol explains a large liver, and the holiday explains dark skin. Together with an M protein and low testosterone they spell POEMS.
Takeaway: POEMS may be primary or secondary to myeloma.

questions.p:
A pathology resident matches translocations to lymphomas. She remembers t(2;5) involves ALK and wonders which lymphoma it belongs to.

Which translocation and lymphoma pairs are correct?
i) t(14;18) and follicular lymphoma
ii) t(11;18) and MALT lymphoma
iii) t(2;5) and Burkitt lymphoma
iv) t(11;14) and mantle cell lymphoma
questions.e:
Correct: C. Follicular is t(14;18), MALT is t(11;18) and mantle cell is t(11;14). These three pairs are correct.
A: t(2;5) is anaplastic large cell lymphoma, not Burkitt.
B: This leaves out the correct MALT pairing.
D: Statement iii) is wrong. Burkitt is t(8;14).
Red herring: Burkitt is the famous translocation lymphoma, which tempts iii). Burkitt is t(8;14). t(2;5) with ALK belongs to anaplastic large cell lymphoma.
Takeaway: Know all five translocations in the notes table.

questions.p:
A radiation oncologist explains why daily fractions work. Between fractions, normal cells fix DNA damage, cells move into more sensitive phases, tumour cells regrow, and hypoxic tumour cells regain oxygen and become more sensitive to the next dose.

Which of the four Rs of radiobiology describes hypoxic cells regaining oxygen?
questions.e:
Correct: D. Reoxygenation of hypoxic cells makes them more sensitive to radiation.
A: Repopulation is regrowth of cells between fractions.
B: Redistribution moves cells into radiosensitive phases of the cell cycle.
C: Repair is the fixing of sublethal damage between fractions.
Red herring: All four Rs happen between fractions, which makes them easy to swap. Regaining oxygen is reoxygenation.
Takeaway: Repair, repopulation, redistribution, reoxygenation.

questions.p:
Lionel, 66, has myeloma. Over two days he has developed back pain, weak legs and trouble passing urine. His calcium is mildly high and his creatinine has risen. He has a known vertebral fracture from 6 months ago that is stable.

Which management is most urgent?
o: Urgent surgery or radiation for cord compression
IV hydration with an intravenous bisphosphonate infusion
questions.e:
Correct: A. New leg weakness and urinary symptoms with back pain suggest cord compression. It is a medical emergency treated with urgent surgery and or radiation.
B: Hydration and bisphosphonates treat hypercalcemia.
C: Hemodialysis is for renal dysfunction.
D: Vertebroplasty is for bone pain and fractures, not cord compression.
Red herring: His high calcium and rising creatinine need treatment too, and the old fracture tempts a planned vertebroplasty. New leg weakness and urinary symptoms mean cord compression, an emergency.
Takeaway: Myeloma emergencies: cord compression, renal dysfunction, plasma cell leukemia.

questions.p:
Walter, 61, has an enlarging neck node. He had a viral illness 2 months ago. Flow cytometry on the excised node shows a monoclonal B-cell population. The report also mentions a mixed inflammatory background.

Which diagnosis does this support?
o: Reactive lymphadenopathy from a viral infection
questions.e:
Correct: C. A monoclonal pattern on flow cytometry is a feature of non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
A: A reactive node gives a polyclonal population.
B: Hodgkin lymphoma shows no monoclonal pattern on flow cytometry.
D: This subtype shows no light chain restriction.
Red herring: The viral illness tempts reactive nodes, and the inflammatory background tempts Hodgkin. A monoclonal B-cell population on flow supports non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
Takeaway: Monoclonal means one clone. Polyclonal means a reactive mix.

questions.p:
Carol, 55, has drooping eyelids and double vision that get worse through the day, and her arms tire when she brushes her hair. Symptoms have crept up over 2 years. She had a mild stroke scare last year that turned out to be a migraine. Her nephew had Hodgkin lymphoma. She smokes.

She has no fevers, night sweats or weight loss. She takes no medications.

Review of systems: no trouble swallowing or breathing at rest, no chest pain and no bleeding. She works as a librarian and has two adult children.

Vitals: HR 76, BP 138/84.
Exam: Bilateral ptosis that worsens on sustained upgaze. Normal reflexes. No lymph nodes.

CT: well-defined anterior mediastinal mass, no lymphadenopathy.

Hb 136 g/L (ref 115-160)
WBC 6.2 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 240 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
LDH normal

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: D. An adult over 40 with a slowly growing anterior mass and myasthenia gravis, a paraneoplastic syndrome, has a thymoma. It is resected without a biopsy first.
A: Neurogenic tumours sit in the posterior mediastinum.
B: Lymphoblastic lymphoma comes on over days.
C: Hodgkin lymphoma affects younger adults and brings nodes and B symptoms.
E: Germ cell tumours present quickly in young men.
Red herring: The past migraine tempts a neurological cause, and her nephew tempts Hodgkin lymphoma. Fatigable weakness with a slow-growing anterior mass and no nodes points to thymoma with myasthenia gravis.
Takeaway: Mediastinal masses: rapid onset suggests lymphoma or germ cell tumour, slow onset suggests thymoma or teratoma.

questions.p:
A trauma patient has a supine AP chest x-ray in the ED because he cannot stand. The mediastinum measures 7 cm wide. The resident remembers "over 6 cm is widened" and wants a CT aorta.

Using the notes, how should this be read?
o: Not widened, since the supine AP cutoff is 8 cm
Widened, since any width over 6 cm counts
Widened, since the supine AP cutoff is 6 cm
Not widened, since every film uses a 10 cm cutoff
questions.e:
Correct: A. A widened mediastinum is over 6 cm on an upright PA film or over 8 cm on a supine AP film. At 7 cm on a supine AP film, it is not widened.
B: The 6 cm cutoff applies to upright PA films.
C: This swaps the PA and AP cutoffs.
D: No 10 cm cutoff is used.
Red herring: The 6 cm cutoff is for upright PA films. A supine AP film magnifies the mediastinum, so the cutoff is 8 cm. At 7 cm, it is not widened.
Takeaway: 6 cm upright PA, 8 cm supine AP.

questions.p:
George, 64, smokes and has lost weight. You feel a firm node just above his left clavicle. He also has a sore tooth and a small scalp cyst.

Which regions drain to this node group?
o: Breast, upper limb and the chest wall
GI tract, GU tract and lungs
Scalp and the skin of the face
Oral cavity, teeth and the upper airway
questions.e:
Correct: B. A node above the clavicle is supraclavicular. It drains the GI tract, GU tract and lungs, so abdominal and thoracic cancers are on the differential.
A: Breast, upper limb and chest wall drain to the axillary nodes.
C: Scalp and skin drain to the preauricular and posterior cervical nodes.
D: The oral cavity drains to the submandibular nodes.
Red herring: The sore tooth and scalp cyst point to regions drained by other node groups. Supraclavicular nodes drain the GI tract, GU tract and lungs.
Takeaway: Supraclavicular nodes are a red flag for malignancy.

questions.p:
Omar, 45, asks why his radiation is split into 20 small daily doses instead of one big dose. His friend told him cancer cells repair damage faster, so small doses give them time to recover.

Why is radiation therapy given as many small daily fractions over several weeks?
o: Cancer cells repair radiation damage faster than normal cells
Slow-growing tumours respond fastest when doses are kept small
Normal tissue repairs damage between fractions better than cancer
Splitting the dose waits until cells leave the sensitive G2-M phase
questions.e:
Correct: C. Fractionation takes advantage of the different repair abilities of normal and malignant tissue. Cancer cells do not repair as well as normal cells.
A: This reverses the repair difference.
B: Fast-growing tumours are more radiosensitive and respond more quickly.
D: Cells are most susceptible in G2-M, not least.
Red herring: His friend has it backwards. Normal cells repair damage between fractions better than cancer cells do.
Takeaway: Fractionation exploits the four Rs.

questions.p:
A node biopsy in a 50-year-old shows atypical lymphoid cells. The pathologist suspects a peripheral T-cell lymphoma rather than DLBCL or Hodgkin lymphoma, and orders stains.

Which panel of immunohistochemistry markers identifies T cells?
questions.e:
Correct: A. Clusters of differentiation identify cell types. T cells carry CD3, CD5 and CD7.
B: CD15 and CD30 mark the Reed-Sternberg cells of classical Hodgkin lymphoma.
C: CD19, CD20 and CD79a mark B cells.
D: CD20 and CD45 are positive in nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma.
Red herring: CD15 and CD30 identify Hodgkin cells, and CD19, CD20 and CD79a identify B cells. T cells carry CD3, CD5 and CD7.
Takeaway: B cells CD19, CD20, CD79a. T cells CD3, CD5, CD7.

questions.p:
A patient with a large anterior mediastinal mass has a hoarse voice, a drooping right eyelid with a small pupil, and low blood pressure. A student adds a fourth possible effect.

Which are recognized complications of a large mediastinal mass?
i) Hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve compression
ii) Ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis from sympathetic chain involvement
iii) Hypotension from compression of the heart
iv) Mydriasis with eyelid retraction from sympathetic chain compression
questions.e:
Correct: B. Hoarseness, Horner syndrome and hypotension from tamponade physiology are all listed effects of a mediastinal mass.
A: This leaves out Horner syndrome.
C: Horner syndrome gives miosis and ptosis, not mydriasis and eyelid retraction.
D: Statement iv) reverses the Horner findings.
Red herring: Statement iv) mentions the sympathetic chain, which sounds right, but it describes the opposite of Horner syndrome.
Takeaway: Horner syndrome is not specific to a mediastinal mass. A Pancoast tumour can cause it.

questions.p:
Walter, 69, has 3 months of back pain, fatigue and constipation. He blames the back pain on shovelling snow. He is thirsty and urinating often, which his doctor first thought was diabetes, but his glucose is normal. He had pneumonia twice this year. He had a PSA test last year that was normal.

He takes hydrochlorothiazide for blood pressure. He does not smoke.

Review of systems: no fevers, bleeding, numbness or tingling. He worked as a farmer and was exposed to pesticides for many years. His wife says he has been more confused this week.

Vitals: HR 94, BP 108/66.
Exam: Dry mucous membranes. Tender lumbar spine.

X-rays: lytic lesions in his spine, pelvis and skull.

Hb 86 g/L (ref 135-170)
WBC 4.0 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 158 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Calcium 2.94 mmol/L
Creatinine 220 µmol/L
Serum M protein present
Marrow plasma cells 35%, monoclonal
Film: rouleaux.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. Monoclonal plasma cells over 10% in the marrow with CRAB organ damage (calcium over 2.52, creatinine over 175, Hb under 100, lytic lesions) is overt multiple myeloma.
A: Plasma cell leukemia needs plasma cells in the blood.
B: MGUS has fewer than 10% plasma cells and no organ damage.
C: Smoldering myeloma has no organ damage.
D: AL amyloidosis deposits light chains in organs, and CRAB with 35% plasma cells defines myeloma.
Red herring: Snow shovelling explains back pain, and hydrochlorothiazide can raise calcium. Neither explains lytic skull lesions, rouleaux and 35% monoclonal plasma cells with CRAB features: multiple myeloma.
Takeaway: Bone pain comes from an imbalance between osteoclasts and osteoblasts.

questions.p:
Harold, 68, has suspected myeloma. A resident orders a set of tests, including one she remembers from a CML patient last week.

Which tests belong in the essential workup for suspected multiple myeloma?
i) Peripheral blood smear for rouleaux
ii) Blood and 24-hour urine protein electrophoresis
iii) Serum free light chain assay
iv) FISH for t(9;22)
questions.e:
Correct: B. Smear for rouleaux, protein electrophoresis of blood and urine, and the serum free light chain assay are all listed myeloma investigations.
A: This leaves out the smear, which shows rouleaux.
C: t(9;22) is not a myeloma FISH target. FISH looks for t(4;14), t(14;16) and del(17p).
D: Statement iv) is wrong for myeloma.
Red herring: FISH is used in myeloma, which makes iv) tempting, but t(9;22) is the CML translocation.
Takeaway: Myeloma FISH: t(4;14), t(14;16), del(17p).

questions.p:
Nora, 65, has a painless neck mass that doubled in size over 4 weeks. She has drenching night sweats and lost 8 kg. She had a dental abscess 6 weeks ago. Her sister had follicular lymphoma. She takes hormone replacement therapy, which she blames for the sweats.

She has had no fevers. She does not smoke.

Review of systems: no cough, abdominal pain or bone pain. She works part-time as a bookkeeper. Her last CBC a year ago was normal.

Vitals: HR 92, BP 126/78, T 37.4°C.
Exam: Large, firm, non-tender neck mass. Nodes in both axillae. Spleen tip palpable.

CT: enlarged nodes in her neck, chest and abdomen.

Hb 114 g/L (ref 115-160)
WBC 8.4 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 290 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
LDH high
Uric acid high
Node biopsy: loss of normal node structure, sheets of large cells with large nuclei and visible nucleoli, and high mitotic activity.
Flow cytometry: monoclonal B cells.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. A painless, rapidly enlarging mass with B symptoms, advanced disease, and large monoclonal B cells that erase the node structure fit DLBCL, the most common NHL.
A: Burkitt shows a starry-sky pattern and is mostly seen in children.
B: Follicular lymphoma is indolent, with a follicular pattern.
C: SLL is indolent, with small cells and smudge cells.
D: Hodgkin lymphoma shows Reed-Sternberg cells and is not monoclonal on flow.
Red herring: Her sister's follicular lymphoma tempts the same diagnosis, but follicular lymphoma is slow. HRT explains some sweats, and the abscess tempts reactive nodes. Rapid growth with large cells that erase the node structure means DLBCL.
Takeaway: DLBCL: CHOP-R, 3 cycles for stage I to II and 6 for stage III to IV.
